reasons: Lake identity is verified for Dunaway v. New York, court U.S. Supreme Court, decided 1979-06-05.
Lake citations match: official 442 U.S. 200, parallels 99 S. Ct. 2248 and 60 L. Ed. 2d 824, vendor cite 1979 U.S. LEXIS 126.
The cached opinion header also shows 442 U.S. 200 (1979) and Supreme Court of United States.
The opinion repeatedly treats Miranda warnings as a central cross-doctrine fact: proper Miranda warnings were given before the statements.
The legal point is not a Miranda holding, but the Fourth Amendment effect of an illegal seizure despite Miranda warnings, supporting Related (cross-doctrine).
residual_risks: No separate home-page taxonomy file is disclosed, so role priority is verified from the opinion text and page context only.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Keep the role as Related, not Key, because the case uses Miranda only in the attenuation/suppression analysis.

reasons: The opinion frames the core issue as whether police violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments by taking Dunaway into custody, transporting him to the station, and detaining him for interrogation without probable cause.

The opinion states: "detention for custodial interrogation...intrudes so severely on interests protected by the Fourth Amendment as necessarily to trigger the traditional safeguards against illegal arrest."
That is a central seizure-of-the-person holding, supporting a Key role.
residual_risks: No separate role-definition file is disclosed for the phrase Key — Progeny.

reasons: The opinion expressly asks whether the connection between the unconstitutional police conduct and the statements/sketches was sufficiently attenuated.
It applies Brown/Wong Sun attenuation factors and concludes no intervening events broke the connection between the illegal detention and confession.
This supports Fruits & Attenuation as a Related cross-doctrine home.
residual_risks: The body Appears on list names The Exclusionary Rule instead of Fruits & Attenuation, although the front matter contains Fruits & Attenuation.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Harmonize the Appears on list with the front matter.

reasons: The opinion holds that police violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments when, without probable cause, they seized Dunaway and transported him to the police station for interrogation.
The text supports the attenuation half: Miranda warnings alone do not cure the Fourth Amendment problem, and no intervening events broke the connection between the illegal detention and confession.
The stated holding is not materially broader than the opinion because it is limited to involuntary station-house custodial interrogation on less than probable cause.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: For maximum precision, say Miranda warnings alone did not attenuate the taint in this station-house illegal-seizure context.
